case_studies.title: Learning the Cost of Reliable Inference
case_studies.abstract: Benchmarking and routing platforms increasingly act as intermediaries connecting large language model providers with end-users. However, providers on these platforms typically use a fixed price per token, preventing users from achieving the most competitive price for their tasks. % workloads. In this work, we design a procurement platform where token prices for each task are driven by provider competition, enabling users to secure competitive pricing for guaranteed quality levels. To this end, the platform sequentially routes queries via a reverse second-price auction that incentivizes model p
case_studies.summary: The paper presents a procurement platform that uses a reverse second-price auction to let users pay the lowest price for LLM inference while guaranteeing a required quality level. By routing each query through a competitive auction, providers set token prices that reflect actual demand, allowing customers to optimise cost for specific workloads. The result is lower spend for high-accuracy inference compared to flat-rate pricing models.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage cloud infrastructure that hosts or consumes LLM services, 1) integrate the auction-based pricing layer into your billing pipeline; 2) define the quality thresholds your workloads need; 3) monitor the platform’s bid outcomes to adjust your procurement strategy and negotiate better rates.

This is highly relevant for IT engineers managing large language model consumption across platforms such as Azure, AWS, and SaaS SaaS. The proposed system can be practically implemented within a 90‑day timeframe as a cost‑optimization micro‑service or as part of an existing MLOps pipeline, offering immediate actionable value. case_studies.title: From Agent Output to Authorized Transition
case_studies.abstract: Agentic engineering systems can edit repositories, run tools and tests, build firmware, synthesize schematics, and prepare deployable or manufacturable artifacts. The assurance problem is therefore shifting from whether an agent can produce an output to whether an engineering lifecycle is justified in acting on claims about that output. Current products and standards provide sandboxes, approvals, hooks, traces, policy enforcement, attestations, bills of materials, and assurance representations, but these capabilities remain fragmented. This paper presents the Agile-V Assurance Spine, a cross-d
case_studies.summary: The paper tackles the problem of verifying that automated engineering agents produce trustworthy outputs. It introduces the Agile‑V Assurance Spine, a framework that unifies sandboxing, policy enforcement, traceability, and attestation to justify acting on agent claims. The result is an integrated assurance model that can be plugged into existing toolchains, but it does not directly impact typical cloud infrastructure management.
case_studies.it_breakdown: Not directly applicable to IT infrastructure work
case_studies.score_reasoning: The paper introduces a novel framework (Agile‑V Assurance Spine) that addresses the growing need for structured assurance around autonomous agents editing code repositories, running tests, and building artifacts—areas directly relevant to modern DevOps and MLOps pipelines. It provides a cross‑cutting set of practices (sandboxes, approvals, hooks, traces, policy enforcement, attestations, BOMs) that can be mapped onto existing CI/CD tools and security tooling. The concepts can be operationalised within the next 90 days by incorporating assurance hooks into GitHub Actions or Azure DevOps, automating policy checks, and generating attestations for container images or firmware builds. While the work is largely conceptual, its actionable recommendations and reference implementation sketches make it highly useful for IT engineers and consultants looking to improve pipeline reliability and compliance, especially for regulated or high‑risk deployments.

case_studies.title: PASTABench: Proactive Assessment of Sequential Trajectories for Agent Safety
case_studies.abstract: As Large Language Models (LLMs) evolve into autonomous agents that alter real-world states, ensuring operational safety across multi-step workflows has become a critical challenge. While recent work has moved beyond single-turn evaluation toward multi-turn paradigms, key limitations persist: step-level methods treat actions in isolation, missing how risks accumulate, while trajectory-level evaluations operate post-hoc, offering no opportunity for timely intervention. To address these limitations, we formalize Decoupled Proactive Safety Monitoring along three dimensions: whether to intervene, w
case_studies.summary: This paper tackles safety for AI agents that act in sequences of steps, a problem that affects any system where automated agents change real‑world states. The authors propose a method to monitor a whole action trajectory in real time, deciding when to intervene before a dangerous outcome occurs. Their prototype shows improved safety in simulated tasks compared to previous step‑by‑step or post‑hoc checks.
case_studies.it_breakdown: Not directly applicable to IT infrastructure work
case_studies.score_reasoning: The paper offers a new approach to proactive safety monitoring of autonomous agents, which is novel in the context of agent safety research. However, its applicability to typical IT infrastructure tasks such as managing Microsoft 365, Google Workspace, or cloud security is limited. The concepts may inform future agentic system deployments but provide little immediate, actionable guidance for everyday IT operations. The overall impact within 90 days is modest.

case_studies.title: The KV Cache Working Set: Online Capacity Planning for LLM Inference Systems
case_studies.abstract: Prefix caching is critical for efficient large language model (LLM) serving, particularly for agentic workloads that repeatedly invoke the model with a growing conversation and tool-use history. By reusing the key-value (KV) states of previously processed prefixes, prefix caching avoids redundant prefill computation. Its effectiveness, however, depends on retaining a sufficiently large set of KV cache states. Provisioning enough cache to preserve all historical KV states is prohibitively expensive and often unnecessary, whereas insufficient capacity can substantially degrade the cache hit rate
case_studies.summary: This work tackles the problem of how much KV cache memory to provision for LLM inference to keep a high hit rate for prefix caching. The authors propose an online capacity‑planning technique that estimates the required cache size from current usage patterns. Applying their method can raise cache hit rates and cut memory costs compared to naïve full‑history storage.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage LLM inference services, step 1: monitor current KV cache hit rates and the number of active prefixes; step 2: run the authors’ capacity‑planning algorithm (or an equivalent implementation) to calculate the minimum cache size needed for a target hit‑rate; step 3: resize your KV cache allocation accordingly and monitor hit‑rates to confirm improvement.
case_studies.score_reasoning: The paper addresses efficient KV cache management for LLM inference, revealing non‑obvious trade‑offs between cache size and hit‑rate that could inform infrastructure scaling decisions for SaaS or edge deployments. For IT engineers, the insights could prompt re‑evaluation of memory allocation for LLM services, but the work is largely conceptual; it does not provide immediate, actionable tools or APIs to deploy within 90 days. Thus the novelty is high, relevance is moderate, and practical value is limited, yielding a combined score of 55. The total exceeds 40, so no low_signal flag is set.

case_studies.title: FDE-Bench: Evaluating LLM Agents for Deployment Environment Configuration
case_studies.abstract: Deployment requires an agent to turn application code into a running system whose services connect, become ready, and remain observable. FDE-Bench evaluates this capability with 136 deployment-configuration tasks spanning Docker images, multi-service Compose stacks, and Kubernetes, in greenfield and diagnose-and-repair modes. Agents submit declarative artifacts that are collected, rebuilt, and redeployed in a pristine environment. Four gated binary check layers measure build, readiness, behavior, and conformance to the deployment specification, using programmatic checks without an LLM judge. A
case_studies.summary: The study tackles the difficulty of turning code into a fully‑functional, observable cloud service by creating a benchmark—FDE‑Bench—made of 136 tasks across Docker, Compose, and Kubernetes. The authors built a system that lets agents output declarative artifacts, which are then automatically built, redeployed and checked against four safety layers to assess build, readiness, behaviour and specification compliance. The result is a repeatable, LLM‑independent evaluation framework that shows how well current agents can handle real‑world deployment scenarios.
case_studies.it_breakdown: Not directly applicable to IT infrastructure work
case_studies.score_reasoning: The paper introduces a new benchmark (FDE‑Bench) that evaluates LLM‑driven agents on real deployment tasks involving Docker, Compose and Kubernetes, which is directly relevant to infrastructure engineers. Its novelty lies in providing a systematic, automated evaluation framework for deployment agents, a topic that is currently underexplored. The benchmark offers actionable insights for engineers looking to assess or improve automation tooling, but the immediate use cases (e.g., building new services or automating existing pipelines) are limited; the main value is in testing and comparison rather than direct deployment. Hence it scores moderately high for relevance and novelty, but lower for rapid 90‑day applicability.

case_studies.title: CART: Closed-Loop Adaptive Red Teaming for Large Language Models
case_studies.abstract: Automated red teaming often replays a fixed set of prompts, which measures known risks but cannot learn from failures found during testing. We present CART (Closed-Loop Adaptive Red Teaming), a framework that uses each result to guide what it tests next. CART begins with broad risk coverage, follows weaknesses that emerge, keeps new probes diverse, and records the evidence and source of every finding. It separates the Challenger that creates tests, the Target being tested, which may be a text-only model or a bounded tool-using agent, and the Judge that evaluates the results, allowing these rol
case_studies.summary: CART is a system that continuously improves red‑team testing of large language models by learning from each failure and generating new, diverse prompts that target emerging weaknesses. It separates three roles—Challenger (creates tests), Target (the LLM or agent), and Judge (evaluates outcomes)—and logs evidence for each finding.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage LLM‑based services, 1) set up a closed‑loop test pipeline that feeds failures back into the Challenger; 2) use the Judge module to automatically score responses for safety and correctness; 3) integrate the logged evidence into your incident‑response playbooks for faster remediation.
case_studies.score_reasoning: CART introduces an adaptive red‑teaming loop for LLMs, which could inform security tooling and risk assessment for SaaS and cloud‑based AI services. The novelty lies in dynamic test generation and evidence tracking, which may catch emergent weaknesses in deployed agents. IT relevance is moderate because the framework targets LLM security rather than direct infrastructure tooling. The value within 90 days is limited: the paper outlines a proof‑of‑concept architecture but does not provide a ready‑to‑use product or SDK that an engineer could deploy immediately. The total score exceeds 40, so no low_signal flag.
